lead: A probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG) attaches a probability to every rewrite rule of a CFG. The probability of a parse tree is the product of the probabilities of the rules it uses. This turns parsing into a search for the most likely tree, not just any tree. Statistical parsers use PCFGs and their relatives to rank readings of news sentences, questions and commands. The same numbers also give a sentence probability, which later scores speech and translation candidates.
prereq: You need 3.1 for rules, 3.2 for treebank counts, and 3.3 for the CYK table.

blocks.text: A probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG) is a context-free grammar plus a probability for every rewrite rule. If a rule is A → α, its probability is written P(A → α). For each nonterminal A, the probabilities of all rules with left side A must sum to 1: Σα P(A → α) = 1. A rule not listed has probability 0. The grammar part is the same as in 3.1; the probabilities rank the trees.
P(T) = Π over every node n in T of P(rule used at n)
blocks.where: P(T) is the probability of tree T; the product runs over nodes, so a rule used at two nodes is multiplied twice.

blocks.text: The model assumes each rule is chosen independently once its parent is fixed. The children of a node are independent given the parent. The choice does not look at the head word, at words outside the span, or at the rest of the sentence. These are strong independence assumptions; they are what makes the dynamic program in the next section possible.

Number the sentence words 1 to n. For a nonterminal A and a span from word i to word j, the inside probability β(i, j, A) is the sum of the probabilities of all subtrees rooted at A that cover exactly words i to j. For a binary rule A → B C, split the span at k.
β(i, j, A) = Σ over rules A → B C and splits k from i to j−1 of P(A → B C) × β(i, k, B) × β(k + 1, j, C)
blocks.where: β(i, j, A) is the inside probability; P(A → B C) is the probability of the binary rule expanded at the root of the span; i and j are word positions; B and C are the two children; k is the last word of the left child's span.

blocks.text: For i = j, β(i, i, A) = P(A → wi) if that rule exists, else 0. Convert the grammar to Chomsky normal form first, as in 3.2. The sentence probability is β(1, n, S). Probabilistic CYK fills the same table as 3.3. It uses sum in the formula above to get the sentence probability. For the most likely tree it uses max:
δ(i, j, A) = max over A → B C and k of δ(i, k, B) × δ(k + 1, j, C) × P(A → B C)
blocks.where: δ(i, j, A) is the probability of the best subtree rooted at A over words i to j; backpointers store the split and rule. The max cell for S is the best tree probability, not the sentence probability.
n is the number of words; |G| is the number of grammar rules. The n³ comes from spans and split points; |G| comes from trying rules.

sections.h3: Estimating the numbers and judging the result

blocks.text: A treebank gives counts. The relative-frequency estimate is P(A → α) = Count(A → α) ÷ Count(A), where Count(A → α) is the number of times that rule is used in the treebank and Count(A) is the number of times A is expanded. Add counts over all trees. This is the maximum-likelihood estimate.
Sparse data is the main problem. Many valid rules never appear, so their probability is 0 and any tree using them gets probability 0. Smoothing, covered in Unit 2, gives unseen rules small counts.

Limitations follow from the independence assumptions. A PCFG is biased toward small trees: when rule probabilities are below 1, every extra node multiplies the tree probability by a number below 1. It has no lexical sensitivity: P(NP → Det N) is the same for 'the boy' and 'the cake'. It is weak on attachment because it has no head word or outside context; see 3.4 and 3.8.

Evaluation compares the constituents (span plus label) in the parser's tree with those in a gold tree. Labelled precision = correct predicted constituents ÷ all predicted constituents. Labelled recall = correct predicted constituents ÷ all gold constituents. F1 = 2 × precision × recall ÷ (precision + recall). Parent annotation and Markovisation are two standard refinements of the nonterminal set; they are named here only.

figure.caption: Each internal node shows the rule used and its probability. The nine probabilities multiply to 0.0036; NP → Det N is used twice, so 0.5 is multiplied twice.

spec.aria: A parse tree for the sentence 'the boy ate the cake' with each internal node showing the rule and its probability; the nine probabilities multiply to 0.0036.

examples.question: For the sentence 'the boy ate the cake', a PCFG has P(S → NP VP) = 1.0, P(NP → Det N) = 0.5, P(VP → V NP) = 0.6, P(Det → the) = 1.0, P(N → boy) = 0.3, P(N → cake) = 0.2, P(V → ate) = 0.4. The sentence has one parse. Find the tree probability and the sentence probability. Show every multiplication.
steps: List the rule at each of the nine nodes in the figure, top to bottom: S → NP VP (1.0); NP → Det N (0.5); Det → the (1.0); N → boy (0.3); VP → V NP (0.6); V → ate (0.4); NP → Det N (0.5); Det → the (1.0); N → cake (0.2).
The grammar gives this sentence only one tree, so the sentence probability is the same 0.0036. With several trees, add the tree probabilities.
examples.answer: The tree probability and the sentence probability are both 0.0036 (dimensionless).

traps: A rule used at two nodes is multiplied twice. A common slip is to count each distinct rule once.
All rules with the same left side must have probabilities summing to 1. P(NP → Det N) = 0.5 and P(NP → Det N PP) = 0.6 cannot both sit in one PCFG.
In CYK, the max entry is the best tree probability. The sentence probability is the sum over all trees, so it can be larger.
Do not add rule probabilities along a single tree; multiply them. Add only when combining different trees for the same sentence.
An unseen rule gives probability 0 and wipes out a tree. Fix this with smoothing, not by silently changing the grammar.

quiz.q: What must be true of P(A → α) for all rules with the same left side A in a PCFG?
quiz.a: They must sum to 1: Σ<sub>α</sub> P(A → α) = 1.

quiz.q: Why does a PCFG often prefer a smaller tree when two trees use rules with probabilities below 1?
quiz.a: Each extra node multiplies the tree probability by a rule probability below 1, so more nodes usually make the product smaller.

quiz.q: A tree uses rules with probabilities 0.9, 0.4 and 0.7. What is P(T)?
A sentence has two parse trees with probabilities 0.004 and 0.001. What is the sentence probability?
Why can a PCFG fail to decide the attachment in 'saw the man with the telescope' reliably?
quiz.a: Its rule probabilities do not see head words or outside context, so they mainly reflect structural frequencies; attachment needs lexical and contextual evidence.

quiz.q: What does β(i, j, A) sum over?
quiz.a: It sums the probabilities of all subtrees rooted at A that cover exactly the words from position i to position j.

quiz.q: The max cell for S is 0.02 and another tree has probability 0.01. Is the sentence probability 0.02? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The sentence probability is the sum over all trees, so with these two trees it is 0.02 + 0.01 = 0.03. The max cell gives only the best tree.

beyond: Not for the exam. PCFG probabilities still appear as features inside modern parsers. Latent-variable PCFGs split nonterminals into finer states learned from data. Neural parsers learn span scores, but their trees are still checked with labelled precision, recall and F1. Search next for the inside-outside algorithm, latent-variable PCFGs, and constituency parsing benchmarks.
